title: Scaling Policies Deep Dive 📈
description: Master the four types of scaling policies – target tracking, step, scheduled, and predictive.

slides.title: Why Scale? And How? 📊
slides.content:
# Match Capacity to Demand

Scaling ensures you have just enough resources – not too few (performance degrades), not too many (waste money).

AWS ASG supports multiple scaling policy types:
- **Target Tracking** – 'Keep CPU at 50%'
- **Step Scaling** – 'Add 2 instances if CPU > 70%, add 4 if > 85%'
- **Scheduled Scaling** – 'Scale to 10 at 9 AM, back to 2 at 6 PM'
- **Predictive Scaling** – machine learning forecasts demand and scales ahead of time.

Multiple policies can be combined; the most aggressive one wins (highest scale‑out takes precedence).

slides.title: Target Tracking: The Set‑and‑Forget Policy 🎯
slides.content:
# Keep Metric at Target

Target tracking policies maintain a specified metric at a target value.

- **Metric examples**: Average CPU Utilization, Average Network In/Out, Request Count Per Target (ALB).
- **How it works**: ASG continuously monitors the metric and adjusts capacity to keep it near the target. No step definitions needed.
- **Best for**: stable, predictable workloads.

Example: 'Keep average CPU at 50%'. If CPU rises to 60%, ASG adds instances; if it drops to 30%, it removes instances.

> Always set a **cooldown period** (default 300 seconds) to prevent rapid oscillations. After a scaling action, ASG waits before taking another action.

quizData.question: You configure a target tracking policy to keep average CPU at 50%. What happens when CPU drops to 20% for 5 minutes?

options.text: ASG may terminate instances (scale in) to bring CPU closer to 50%, subject to cooldown and min capacity
The policy will wait for manual approval

quizData.explanation: Target tracking can scale in as well as scale out. It will reduce instance count to align with the target metric, respecting minimum capacity.

slides.title: Step Scaling: Granular Control 🪜
slides.content:
# Respond to Changing Intensity

Step scaling policies let you define different responses based on the magnitude of the breach.

- Define CloudWatch alarms at different thresholds.
- Each breach step triggers a specific adjustment (e.g., add 1 instance, add 3 instances, remove 1 instance).
- You can use **metric intervals** (lower bound, upper bound) or simple breach.

Example steps for CPU:
- 60‑70%: add 1 instance
- 70‑85%: add 2 instances
- 85%+: add 4 instances

More complex to configure than target tracking, but gives you precise control.

slides.title: Scheduled Scaling: Time‑Based 📅
slides.content:
# Know Your Peaks

If your traffic follows a predictable pattern (e.g., e‑commerce site peak hours 9‑5), use scheduled scaling.

- Set the desired capacity at specific times (cron expressions).
- Can specify min/max/desired individually per schedule.
- Best combined with dynamic scaling for the unexpected surges within the scheduled window.

Example: 'At 9 AM weekdays, set desired=10, min=5, max=20. At 6 PM, set desired=2, min=1, max=5.'

slides.title: Predictive Scaling: AI‑Driven 🤖
slides.content:
# Scale Before the Spike

Predictive Scaling uses machine learning to analyse historical load and forecast future demand. It proactively scales capacity ahead of anticipated spikes.

- Works with target tracking policy (forecast only).
- Only scales out (not in), works on daily/weekly patterns.
- Requires at least 24 hours of historical data.

Best for applications with repeating patterns (workday mornings, Black Friday). Combined with dynamic scaling, it can pre‑warm capacity so you never hit a cold start delay.

slides.title: Cooldown, Warm‑Up & Instance Scale‑In Protection 🛡️
slides.content:
# Fine‑Tune Timing

- **Cooldown Period** (default 300s): after a scaling action, ASG waits before evaluating metrics again. Prevents thrashing.
- **Instance Warm‑Up**: when a new instance launches, it may need time to initialise (download packages, warm caches). ASG ignores metrics from that instance until warm‑up completes.
- **Scale‑In Protection**: you can protect specific instances from termination (e.g., a long‑running batch job). The ASG won't terminate protected instances during scale‑in.
- **Termination Policy**: determines which instances are terminated first when scaling in (oldest launch template, closest to next billing hour, etc.).
